readings: R1=Distinct over non-missing source text; R2=Distinct over non-missing stored values; R+=Distinct over all cells, empty counts as one value
why: A csv-module reference with len(set(column)) counts the empty string as a value while a pandas nunique excludes it, and a fixture with blanks will pin one of them.

readings: R1=File with no delimiter is a valid one-column table; R+=No inferable delimiter means non-tabular, HTTP 400
why: A non-tabular fixture is often multi-line prose or HTML, which R1 accepts as a one-column table, and csv.Sniffer in a reference implementation raises on delimiter-free text.

readings: R1=all ints integer, all floats float, int/float mix number, any text text, over non-missing; R2=numeric columns always number; R+=mixed numeric/text is number not text
why: Four labels with no definition means the reference picked a lattice the spec never states, so even the most natural one is a coin-weighted guess on mixed columns.

readings: R1=force= is a value and is HTTP 400; only a bare force is presence; R2=Empty string is presence, any non-empty value is HTTP 400
why: A Python reference implementation cannot tell ?force from ?force= through its query parser, so its tests will treat the empty value as presence while asserting 400 only for force=1 or force=true.

readings: R1=int() then float() style: signs, exponents and leading zeros all numbers, non-finite stay text; R2=strict grammar: no leading zeros, no exponent, no plus; R3=signs and exponents numbers, leading zeros text
why: The spec carves out only time-like values, which suggests a try-int-then-float reference, but a zip-code style 007 fixture expecting text is a live possibility.

readings: R1=Pad short rows with empty strings, truncate long rows; R+=Reject ragged file as non-tabular; R++=Rows keep their natural length
why: A pandas-based reference 400s on long rows and pads short ones with null, so any ragged fixture can disagree with empty-string padding.

readings: R1=only the header-plus-one-data-row rule; R2=row rule plus rejecting empty, binary, markup and JSON payloads; R3=also require at least two columns
why: The natural non-tabular fixture is an HTML page or binary blob, which usually has more than one line and slips past a pure row-count rule.

readings: R1=Empty charset equals omitted, fall through to detection; R+=Empty charset is malformed, 400
why: A malformed-charset fixture is usually a bogus codec name, and args.get('charset') falsiness makes empty-as-omitted the reference-natural path, but an empty-string edge test is plausible.

readings: R1=Spreadsheet summary carries filetype, row_count and column_count; R+=Spreadsheet summary is filetype only
why: A test asserting dataset_summary == {'filetype': 'excel'} exactly is a real possibility given the word 'only', though a key lookup is more common.

readings: R1=spreadsheet ignores charset entirely, even an unknown codec name gives 200; R2=codec name still validated for any source, only decode is CSV-only; R3=as R1 but bad charset plus unreachable source still 400
why: applies and validates only for text CSV sources reads like a sentence written to back a test that an xlsx with a bogus charset ingests, so a name check on spreadsheets is the exposed side.

readings: R1=strict: any non-blank non-comment line that is not KEY=VALUE, or an unknown key, fails startup; R2=permissive: unparseable lines and unknown keys ignored; R3=malformed lines fail but unknown keys are ignored; all split at first = and trim
why: Tests most likely exercise bad values (a non-integer size, a bad boolean) where every reading agrees, but a stray unknown key or a bare line in a fixture would split the strict and permissive readings.

readings: R1=force present twice is 400; R2=a repeated presence flag is idempotent and forces
why: An author who wrote "if present once" was probably thinking of the repeat and pairing it with the repeated-control 400, but the case may go untested.

readings: R1=a bad _sort is still 400 when _sort_desc is present; R+=a losing _sort is ignored
why: The 400 rule is unconditional, but a reference written as "if _sort_desc: use it, elif _sort: ..." never looks at the loser, and the combination is plausible in a precedence test.

readings: R1=Unknown key fails startup; R2=Unknown key ignored
why: Invalid-config fixtures are usually a bad value or a non KEY=VALUE line, so neither reading is likely exercised, but an extra-key-tolerated test is likelier than an extra-key-rejected one.

readings: R1=total order, numbers numerically first then text by code point; R2=compare every value as its string form; R3=raise or 500 on mixed columns
why: A numeric column must sort 2 before 10 to satisfy the type rules, but what the reference does on a genuinely mixed column is unknowable and could be probed.

readings: R1=Drop every blank or all-whitespace line before the two-row check; R2=Keep interior blank lines as empty rows, drop trailing newline only; R3=Every empty record kept as a row of empty strings, trailing newline creates none
why: All readings ignore the trailing newline, which is what a header-only 400 test exercises; interior blank lines are unlikely in author-generated fixtures, and if present a csv.reader-based reference most naturally skips them.

readings: R1=Id from URL alone; cache hit only when charset matches, else re-ingest and replace; R2=Id from URL alone; every repeat re-fetches and overwrites
why: A cache test naturally counts fetches at the mock origin and expects one, which R2 fails; a same-URL-different-charset test is improbable so R1's re-ingest choice is safe either way.

readings: R1=Unset means no file; a set path that cannot be read exits; empty string exits; R2=Same, but empty string treated as unset; R+=Missing file is tolerated, defaults apply
why: The spec pairs read failure with exit, so a test pointing DATAGATE_CONFIG at a missing path most naturally expects a non-zero exit; the empty-string subcase is unlikely to be tested.

readings: R1=valid codec that cannot decode the bytes is 400; R2=decode leniently with replacement and answer 200
why: A reference that does bytes.decode(charset) in a try block yields 400 without extra effort, but the error row is worded about the parameter and the case may not be probed at all.

readings: R1=export applies the default _size of 100 like /datasets; R+=export returns all rows by default
why: The same pagination is unqualified, but an author who thinks of export as a download may never write the over-100-rows fixture, and if they do a shared pipeline gives 100.

readings: R1=BOM or strict UTF-8 decode, else latin-1, no statistical detector; R+=Statistical detector such as chardet
why: UTF-8 and latin-1 fixtures decode the same under both; the residual risk is a cp1252 fixture whose 0x80-0x9F bytes a chardet-based reference decoded as smart quotes.

readings: R1=Repeated enrich=yes is not exact, enrichment off; R2=Every occurrence yes still enriches; R+=Repeat is 400
why: Repetition is probably not fixtured, and if it is, 'only exact' plus 'all other states' points to off rather than an error.

readings: R1=exactly the eight spellings after case folding, no trim, empty string fails startup; R2=case-fold after trimming whitespace, empty value means unset/default
why: Checkpoint 6 spells out "case-insensitive, trimmed" for every boolean, so a test with padded whitespace is plausible and only no-trim implementations lose it; empty values are unlikely to be probed.

readings: R1=Empty string is an ordinary value: exact matches empty cells, contains matches all; R+=Empty filter value is HTTP 400
why: The filter error table is closed and omits empty values, so a test author asserting 400 would be inventing a rule; the case is more likely untested than tested.

readings: R1=consistency count over comma, semicolon, tab and pipe; R2=csv.Sniffer; R3=rectangularity scoring over exactly comma, semicolon, tab
why: Tests will feed comma, semicolon and tab files, likely with time-like colons and quoted delimiters; an unrestricted Sniffer is the reading that can pick a wrong character.

readings: R1=a re-ingestion without enrich stores the dataset non-enriched; R+=enrichment is a one-way latch
why: Requests without re-ingestion do not change stored state implies re-ingestions do, but the successful-downgrade path is the kind of case an author leaves untested.

readings: R1=render every cell to text (integral numbers without .0, TRUE/FALSE, ISO dates) then run CSV inference; R+=map native cell types directly
why: Number and text cells agree either way; date and boolean cells, and .xls floats for whole numbers, are where an author's fixture could disagree with either reading.

readings: R1=405 with the JSON envelope; R+=404 with the JSON envelope
why: A test most likely asserts only a JSON error for a wrong method, and if it pins a code 405 is what a router gives.

readings: R1=Strip one leading U+FEFF after decoding, even with explicit charset=utf-8; R+=BOM kept as data when charset given explicitly
why: A BOM is the textbook unambiguous marker and any author with a BOM fixture expects columns[0]=='id'; explicit-charset-plus-BOM is rarely fixtured.

readings: R1=Render stored values, numbers by JSON spelling, strings verbatim; R2=Re-emit source cell text verbatim
why: Readings differ only on 007, 1.50 or padded cells, which plain fixtures lack, and 'semantically-correct' suggests the checker parses and compares by value.

readings: R1=Empty or whitespace-only cell is missing, padding included; R2=Only the empty string is missing; R+=NA-style sentinels also missing
why: Fixtures use blank cells where R1 and R2 agree; the tail risk is a pandas-based reference that swallowed 'NA' or 'null'.

readings: R1=compare against the JSON text of the stored value; R2=numeric cells never match string comparators; R3=compare against the original source text
why: An exact filter on a numeric column is a likely test and R2 silently returns nothing there, while R1 and R3 only diverge on non-canonical numerals tests rarely use.

readings: R1=exactly text/csv with no parameters, UTF-8 body; R2=text/csv; charset=utf-8
why: Most tests will check the media type with startswith or contains, but a literal equality against the quoted header is plausible and only the bare value survives it.

readings: R1=a line that is neither KEY=VALUE, blank nor comment is invalid config and exits; R2=unparseable lines are skipped
why: Invalid config ... exits is most naturally tested with a bad value, but a garbage line is the next candidate and only fail-fast survives it.

readings: R1=any positive _size is honoured, 200 returns 200 rows; R2=100 is a hard ceiling; R3=_size above 100 is 400
why: If it exceeds available rows, return all and "default 100" read as a knob, not a cap, and a large-dataset probe would most likely expect the requested count.

readings: R1=Unset means default on; empty string is an invalid value and fails startup; R2=Unset and empty string both mean the default
why: Tests will cover unset (must start, caches) and garbage values (must fail); an empty string is rarely worth a test and the trimmed rule makes it as likely rejected as accepted.

readings: R1=Header cells returned verbatim in source order; R+=Deduplicate or synthesise names for repeated and empty headers
why: Nothing in the spec licenses renaming, so a test with an odd header would compare against the raw cells; most fixtures have clean headers anyway.

readings: R1=Padded numerics become numbers; non-numeric text kept verbatim; R+=Padded cell stays a string
why: Python's float and int accept surrounding whitespace, so a reference implementation converts " 42 " to 42 without trying, and tests derived from it agree.

readings: R1=injected row number owns the rowid key, columns still verbatim; R+=source column keeps the key
why: Almost certainly untested; if tested, the unconditional "includes rowid (1-based row number)" favours the injected value.

readings: R1=Access-Control-Allow-Origin * on every response including errors, OPTIONS answered; R2=same plus allow-methods, allow-headers, expose-headers and max-age on every response; R3=echo the request Origin
why: Tests will look for Access-Control-Allow-Origin on a response, probably "*", and the extra headers cost nothing while echoing Origin can fail a test that sends none.

readings: R1=resolve the dataset first, unknown id is 404; R2=validate controls first, 400; R3=either
why: The 404 rule is unconditional and _sort validation needs the dataset, so a reference resolves first; the combination is unlikely to be tested.

readings: R1=Toggles still validated on export, bogus value is 400, valid value no-op; R2=Toggles ignored outright on export
why: The fixture is almost surely _shape=objects yielding identical CSV; a bogus-value-on-export assertion is rare and would favour 400 via shared parsing.

readings: R1=Numeric means float() accepts it, nan and inf allowed; R2=Strict decimal grammar, nan and inf are 400
why: The spec names float parse, so a reference uses float(); the fixture is abc giving 400, and a nan probe is unlikely but would side with R1.

readings: R1=store is the cache keyed by id from source URL, charset must match for a hit; R2=keyed on source URL alone, charset ignored on a hit; R3=keyed on URL alone but a differing charset re-decodes
why: Tests will most naturally count downloads for a repeated identical URL and assert no expiry within a run, which every reading satisfies; a charset-varying cache probe is unlikely.

readings: R1=label-boundary suffix match, equal or ends with dot plus suffix, leading dot on entries stripped; R+=plain string endswith
why: domain-boundary rules exists to make notexample.com fail against example.com, which is exactly the negative case a test author would write.

readings: R1=bytes of the fetched body or the uploaded file part; R2=declared Content-Length or the whole request body; R3=size of the parsed dataset
why: file size = limit accepted invites a test with a file of exactly the limit, which measuring the multipart envelope would wrongly reject.

readings: R1=https plus the Host header verbatim, port included, same path; R2=Host with the port stripped; R3=server bind address; R+=plaintext requests rejected under REQUIRE_TLS
why: Test clients address 127.0.0.1:port, so "request host" is that string verbatim and stripping the port breaks the expected URL, while refusing plaintext would break the harness itself.

readings: R1=unknown parameters ignored, repeated or not; R2=unknown parameters are 400; R3=unknown underscore names 400, others ignored
why: Checkpoint 3 says params without _ and without __ are ignored, and no error row covers unknown names; only an unknown _foo probe could split R1 from R3.

readings: R1=Single key describing the leftmost column of that name; R2=Single key describing the rightmost column
why: An enriched fixture with a repeated header is an unlikely test, and either collapse yields a well-formed object with the same key set.

readings: R1=Allowlist 403 first, then param checks, then fetch 404, then size 400, then parse; R2=Same ordering with upload's 415 and multipart 400 preceding the size check
why: Combined-fault requests are rarely tested beyond 403 before routing, and every reading puts the allowlist first and the size check after the bytes exist.

readings: R1=Id is a pure function of the URL; rows live in memory, 404 after restart; R2=Persist to disk so rows survive restart; R+=Counter-based id stable within one process only
why: At this checkpoint tests are unlikely to restart the server, and a hash-of-URL id satisfies any cross-process determinism check whether or not rows persist.

readings: R1=Enrichment flag and metadata persisted with the dataset, served after restart; R+=Metadata in memory only, dataset returns non-enriched after restart
why: Enrichment is called stored state and persisted datasets must survive, so any restart test on an enriched dataset expects the metadata back.

readings: R1=Filter resolves to the first column with that name; R+=Ambiguous name is HTTP 400
why: The only column-resolution error listed is unknown column, and a repeated-header filter fixture is unlikely to be tested at all.

readings: R1=Documented verb only; other methods get 405 in the JSON envelope; R2=Other methods get some JSON error, status unasserted
why: Wrong-method tests on the new routes are uncommon and a 405 JSON envelope satisfies any generic error assertion that might exist.

readings: R1=Rows, columns, source, charset all persist and /convert after restart is a cache hit; R2=Datasets persist and stay queryable, cache is per process; R3=One JSON file per dataset, unreadable files skipped at startup
why: A restart test reuses the directory and expects GET /datasets/<id> to answer; whether the following /convert re-downloads is unlikely to be counted.

readings: R1=Sort by the first column carrying that name; R+=Ambiguous name is HTTP 400
why: The name is known so the listed 400 does not apply, and a duplicate-header sort fixture is unlikely to appear in the suite.

readings: R1=Underscore-prefixed filter-shaped params are unknown controls and ignored; such columns unfilterable; R+=Treated as a filter on the underscore column
why: The control-param rule is by spelling, and a source column starting with underscore is an unlikely fixture.

readings: R1=empty STORAGE_DIR fails startup; R+=empty means unset, use the default
why: Nothing in the spec or a plausible fixture sets STORAGE_DIR to the empty string.

readings: R1=RFC 4180 quoting honoured and quoting does not affect typing, "1" becomes 1; R+=a quoted number stays text
why: Python's csv module drops the quotes before inference, which is what a reference would do.

readings: R1=re-fetch and replace on every convert until checkpoint 5, cached thereafter; R+=serve from cache from the first checkpoint
why: Early tests key on the endpoint being stable; only a refresh fixture would separate the readings, and checkpoint 5 settles it.

readings: R1=trim trailing empty rows and columns, then require header plus one row; R+=take the declared range verbatim
why: Generated fixtures rarely carry phantom trailing cells, and trimming is what makes "header + at least one data row" a content test.

readings: R1=Split on comma from file or env, trim items, drop empties; R+=Env value is opaque, no splitting
why: Fixtures will use a plain comma list from either source and R1 handles both; nobody writes a suffix with spaces.

readings: R1=Empty value is no allowlist, all pass; R+=Empty list active, 403 everything; R++=Empty value fails startup
why: An explicitly empty ORIGIN_ALLOWLIST is an unlikely fixture and pass-through is what a reference reading 'unset' as falsy does.

readings: R1=exact case-sensitive untrimmed match of hide, lists, objects; R+=case-insensitive or trimmed match
why: Tests for "any other value" will use a clearly wrong word, and a reference doing an exact string compare is the default; a case-folded probe is improbable.

readings: R1=no new status, ingestion failures keep their codes and prior enriched state is preserved; R2=a metadata computation failure is HTTP 500 in the envelope
why: A test author can hardly induce a genuine metadata-compute failure, so the only likely probe is a failed forced re-ingest leaving the prior enriched dataset intact, which both readings pass.

readings: R1=force with a value is 400 regardless of cache setting; R2=force is ignored entirely when caching is disabled
why: Any force value is HTTP 400 is unconditional and validation-before-effect is the natural implementation; the combined case is a second-tier test at most.

readings: R1=header is 1, first data row is 2, counted over parsed records; R+=first data row is 1; R+=physical file lines
why: 1-based ... starting at the header is explicit, and blank-line fixtures that would separate record from line counting are unlikely.

readings: R1=Only byte-exact enrich=yes enables; every other state including repeats is silently off; R+=Wrong value or repeated enrich is HTTP 400
why: The sentence "All other states keep enrichment off" is unconditional, so tests for enrich=YES or enrich=no will expect 200 without metadata.

readings: R1=Process exits non-zero with a stderr message and never binds the port
why: A harness can only observe the exit status and the closed port, and no reading here exits zero or keeps serving.

readings: R1=Only http or https with a non-empty host, no whitespace or control chars, is valid; else 400; R+=Anything urlparse accepts is valid
why: A test author writing "Invalid URL 400" will send not-a-url or a scheme-less string, both 400 under R1, and the 404 row presupposes an HTTP fetch.

readings: R1=strip surrounding whitespace, lowercase, must be one of the eight spellings; R+=no trimming, whitespace makes the value invalid
why: The checkpoint-6 wording says "trimmed" outright, and a test author who wrote that word would assert " TRUE " is accepted if they probe whitespace at all.

readings: R1=with caching on, a repeat convert is served from the store with no download; R+=may re-download at will
why: The section defines CACHE_ENABLED and force as the only ways to trigger a download, so the natural test counts origin hits and expects one.

readings: R1=last occurrence wins; R+=duplicate key fails startup
why: Last-wins is what every KEY=VALUE format does and a duplicate-key fixture is an unlikely test.

readings: R1=enrich is ignored on upload, datasets and export; R+=enrich elsewhere is 400
why: Applies only on /convert reads as scope, and unknown parameters are ignored everywhere else in the spec.

readings: R1=bare setting names in the environment, env over file over defaults; R+=DATAGATE_-prefixed names
why: Checkpoint 5 already names the bare CACHE_ENABLED variable, so tests set the unprefixed names.

readings: R1=a failed re-ingestion leaves the prior dataset queryable in every case; R+=with caching disabled a failure clears the stored dataset
why: The failure guarantee is written for force, and a reference that replaces only on success behaves the same with caching off.

readings: R1=split on the last __ (rpartition); R+=split on the first __
why: Fixtures almost certainly use plain column names, and a bogus comparator is 400 under both splits.

readings: R1=use cached values, uncached formula becomes empty, never evaluate; R+=export the formula text
why: The spec says the behaviour is not required, so at most a well-formed response is asserted.

readings: R1=only multipart/form-data counts, everything else 415; R2=any multipart/* counts, multipart/mixed is malformed 400
why: Tests will send JSON or plain text for 415 and a broken form body for 400; multipart/mixed is an unlikely fixture.

readings: R1=a stable implementation-defined directory with datasets persisted as files; R2=a fresh temporary directory per process
why: Persistence tests will set STORAGE_DIR explicitly, so the default is barely observable.

readings: R1=file wins when both are present, both is not an error; R+=both present is 400
why: The only documented 400 is "missing both", and a fixture with both parts is unlikely.

readings: R1=filetype is the literal csv; R+=media type text/csv
why: The excel literal fixes the vocabulary as bare format words, so a test on the CSV side almost surely asserts 'csv'.

readings: R1=Trimmed decimal digits with optional plus, negatives floats suffixes invalid at startup; R+=Anything int() accepts
why: Fixtures set a plain integer and check equal-to and over-limit bodies; a weird spelling test is unlikely and R1 rejects the obvious garbage.

readings: R1=float() on the stored value's text decides, failure skips the row; R2=Any stored non-JSON-number is skipped
why: The two differ only on text that float-parses but was stored as text, which no ordinary fixture contains.

readings: R1=Identical repeats of a control are still 400, other names may repeat; R2=Repeated source uses the first value; R+=Repeated source is 400
why: The fixture is a repeated _size, which is 400 under every reading; repeated source is rarely tested.

readings: R1=Valid no-op under lists; R+=400 under lists
why: The only listed toggle error is a non-hide value, and a reference that checks the value then drops the key never errors under lists.

readings: R1=ASCII digits with optional sign then range check; R2=ASCII digits only; R+=Anything int() accepts
why: Fixtures are 0, -1, abc and 1.5, all rejected under every reading; +5 or padded spellings are not fixtured.

readings: R1=Resolve the dataset first, 404; R+=Validate filters first, 400
why: Unknown column cannot be judged without the dataset's header, so a reference resolves the id first, and the combination is seldom fixtured.

readings: R1=exact, case-sensitive match of the four lowercase names; R+=case-insensitive match
why: The invalid-comparator test will almost surely use a made-up name rather than uppercase, and a reference implementation most naturally does a case-sensitive set lookup.

readings: R1=hash of the exact source string, no normalisation; R+=counter with a persisted URL-to-id table
why: Tests only observe that identical URLs share an endpoint, different URLs differ, and datasets survive restart, all of which a deterministic hash satisfies.

readings: R1=enrich never changes the id or the endpoint, upgrades the stored dataset in place; R+=enriched ingestion yields a distinct id
why: upgrades stored state and the unconditional same-URL-same-id rule make a shared endpoint the assertion a test author would naturally make.

readings: R1=first sheet in stored workbook order; R2=the active sheet at save time
why: Test workbooks built with openpyxl have sheet 0 active by default, so both readings usually coincide and workbook order is what "first" means.

readings: R1=rowid always carries the row number, duplicate names collapse last-wins, columns untouched; R+=rename the synthetic key on collision
why: Neither collision is a likely fixture, and the unconditional "includes rowid" makes the row number the safe value if one is.

readings: R1=sorted with reverse=True, ties keep source order; R+=exact reverse of the ascending result
why: Stable is a term of art for ties keeping input order, and the reference almost certainly calls sorted with reverse.

readings: R1=any multipart field named file or attachment carries the payload, filename optional; R2=only a part with a filename counts
why: Test clients send files with a filename, so both readings pass the likely fixtures; the spec says "field" and never mentions a filename.

readings: R1=the full column__comparator name repeated is 400, different comparators on one column are ANDed; R+=any column named twice is 400
why: A range query on one column is the obvious use of "Multiple filters are ANDed", so tests will expect it to work and expect a literal repeat to be 400.

readings: R1=environment overrides file overrides defaults, resolved per key; R+=defaults outrank both sources
why: Any other direction makes the whole configuration section inert, and a per-key env-over-file test is the obvious one to write.

readings: R1=zero-byte file part is HTTP 400 in the JSON envelope; R+=empty upload succeeds as an empty dataset
why: Both the missing-field and the header-plus-data-row rules land on 400, and tests rarely pin the message.

readings: R1=404 in the standard JSON envelope, query validated after id resolution; R+=CSV or empty error body
why: all errors use the standard JSON envelope plus the existing unknown-id rule leave 404 JSON as the only defensible answer.

readings: R1=row_count and column_count describe the whole stored dataset, fixed at ingestion; R2=they describe the current filtered page
why: Re-ingestion recomputes metadata from current source bytes fixes the computation at ingestion, and a test paging an enriched dataset would expect the counts to hold.

readings: R1=Comment is a whole line whose first non-blank char is hash; R2=Hash or semicolon may start a comment line
why: Any config fixture with comments will use leading hash lines, which both readings ignore, and a semicolon data line is not something a test would write.

readings: R1=Sniff bytes: OLE2 is xls, ZIP workbook is xlsx, else CSV; name and type are hints at most; R+=Decide from URL extension or upload filename
why: Content sniffing accepts every fixture an extension-based test would serve, and also the extensionless URLs a test server may use.

readings: R1=Redirects followed; final status 400 or above and any transport failure map to 404; 2xx with bad body is the 400 path
why: A mock origin returning 404 or 500 is the natural test and both are 404 here; a redirect fixture is improbable.

readings: R1=Setting only shapes the returned endpoint URLs; plaintext requests still served
why: The test harness has no TLS listener, so the only checkable behaviour is the https absolute endpoint returned over plain HTTP.

readings: R1=Create recursively; a path that cannot become a directory fails startup
why: Tests will give a fresh temp path and expect it created; a path that exists as a file, if tested, pairs with the startup-failure row.

readings: R1=UTF-8, comma delimiter, RFC 4180 quoting, any line terminator; R+=echo the source delimiter
why: text/csv with no delimiter parameter is comma-separated, and a test helper will read the export with a default csv reader.

readings: R1=Hash of the file bytes only, filename field and charset excluded; R+=Filename or charset mixed into the hash
why: The sentence names bytes alone, and the likely fixture is the same bytes under a second filename yielding the same id.

readings: R1=any Referer that yields no hostname is 403, empty treated as missing; R+=unparseable Referer is 400
why: The procedure ends in "Otherwise return HTTP 403" and the error table has no 400 row for this check.

readings: R1=Top-level fields of the /datasets/<id> JSON only; /convert body and export unchanged
why: The section is headed "Enriched query output" and pins the /convert body as unchanged, so tests look for the fields in the query response alone.

readings: R1=fixed 100 with no override parameter, unknown params ignored; R2=a limit parameter clamped to 100
why: Both keep "at most 100" true, and _size arrives in checkpoint 2 to replace either.

readings: R1=a cache hit is not size-checked; R+=re-check the recorded size on a hit
why: The limit is a startup setting, so within one process a cached dataset was already checked at ingestion.

readings: R1=Whole response identical: status, body, headers, no cache marker; R+=Body identical but a cache header added
why: Tests can only compare status and body of two /convert calls, which every reading satisfies; R1 is the safe superset.

readings: R1=Literally every request before routing, unknown paths and OPTIONS included; R+=Only data routes or preflight exempt
why: Allowlist fixtures hit /convert or /datasets with and without Referer, where all readings agree.

readings: R1=A failed ingestion in any mode returns the error and leaves stored data intact; R+=With cache disabled a failure empties the id
why: The spelled-out forced case is what gets fixtured and R1 satisfies it and its disabled-cache twin.

readings: R1=Leading underscore never a filter, contains double underscore is a validated filter, else ignored
why: All runs converge and the fixtures (foo=bar ignored, bad__exact 400) are exactly what R1 produces.

readings: R1=force parsed and validated only on /convert, ignored elsewhere; R+=force validated on every route
why: The section is about the /convert cache, so force=1 is tested there and nowhere else.

readings: R1=total counts filtered rows before pagination, independent of sort, size, offset and shape, removed by _total=hide
why: Every sentence about total in the spec converges on this one value and nothing plausible competes with it.

readings: R1=Both xls and xlsx report filetype excel, decided from bytes
why: The spec offers exactly one label for spreadsheets and never distinguishes the two workbook formats in a response.

readings: R1=Header row of column names first, then data rows, even with zero rows
why: Export columns follow source column order is only observable with a header, and a test parsing the CSV would read column names from it.

readings: R1=Server-side wall-clock budget of several seconds on the whole query; R2=No timeout implemented, treated as untestable
why: No input in a test can force a slow query, so the row is unreachable; all readings return 200 for ordinary filtered queries.

readings: R1=Unusable container magic reports unrecognized format, bad text reports non-tabular; R2=Both branches are one 400 differing only in message
why: Both branches are 400 with the standard envelope, so the distinction is invisible to any status-based test.

readings: R1=First 100 rows in source order
why: In source order plus the determinism section leaves no other window a test could assert.

readings: R1=Fixed deterministic order, every case 400 so only the message differs
why: Every combination is 400 with the same envelope and tests do not assert message text.

readings: R1=H:MM with optional seconds and fraction stays text, everything non-numeric stays text anyway
why: Colon-bearing values never match a number grammar, so the fixture passes under any reading.

readings: R1=monotonic-clock milliseconds around the handler, float, clamped at zero
why: Tests can only assert presence, type and non-negativity, which every sane implementation meets.

readings: R1=Column names are always strings; R+=Header cells type-inferred
why: The schema shows quoted column names and no reference would emit a numeric column name.
